sweeps.angle: Chicago neighborhood-walk content on TikTok — for each named neighborhood, what TikTok actually shows people doing (walk a specific street, hit specific stops) rather than generic tourism copy.
sweeps.coverage_note: Ran the 6 required queries plus 6 follow-ups (12 total). Coverage is uneven across the 8 requested neighborhoods: Pilsen, Logan Square, West Loop, and Chinatown returned genuine named spots and route detail. Wicker Park, Andersonville, and especially Hyde Park returned mostly generic 'discover' topic pages (auto-generated TikTok hashtag/search landing pages) rather than verified viral videos or named creators — I've marked these 'weak' and said so rather than inventing specifics. I could not directly view TikTok video content (search results are text summaries of what TikTok's own search/discover pages surface, not full video transcripts), so 'why it went viral' reasoning is inferred from what's described, not confirmed via watching the clips. No entries were fabricated; where evidence was thin I said so in evidence_strength and tiktok_evidence rather than padding it. A next pass should run neighborhood+specific-landmark queries (e.g. "University of Chicago tiktok", "Museum of Science and Industry tiktok", "Andersonville Clark Street tiktok") to strengthen the three weak neighborhoods.

sweeps.angle: Chicago TikTok skyline/rooftop/photo-spot research — exact vantage points, best time of day, and free-vs-paid status
sweeps.coverage_note: Ran 10 WebSearch queries total (exceeds the 6 requested). Strong direct TikTok evidence (specific videos/creators cited by name) exists for: Adler Planetarium, Ping Tom Memorial Park, Chicagohenge, and the Indiana Dunes mirage phenomenon, plus the @secret.chicago hidden hiking spot (though that trail's exact name/location was never disclosed in search results — would need to watch the video directly to geolocate it). Rooftop bars (Cindy's, LondonHouse/Terrace 16, Tetto, Z Bar, VU) were named in aggregated search-engine summaries of TikTok content but I could not pull individual video URLs for each to verify view counts or exact creator claims — evidence there is real but softer than the photo-spot entries. The bridge/lagoon entries (Kinzie St, Fullerton Ave, South Pond) came from photography-guide roundup articles rather than confirmed TikTok posts, so I've flagged those as weak evidence — they are commonly recommended skyline vantage points but I did not find a TikTok-specific citation proving they went viral there specifically, as distinct from being generically popular photo spots. I did not verify current wait times, prices, or whether any of these spots/venues have closed or changed since the underlying TikTok posts (some dated 2024-2025). No fabricated evidence — every entry's tiktok_evidence field states plainly what was and wasn't found.

sweeps.angle: Chicago attractions and experiences that TikTok specifically amplifies (2024-2026) — distinct from a standard guidebook list. Focus is on what makes each spot "TikTok-native": glass-floor/ledge thrill moments, immersive photo-op museums, a viral historian's tour brand, a literal sidewalk meme that became a pilgrimage site, and skyline-view experiences (boat/kayak/observation deck) that are inherently short-vertical-video-shaped.
sweeps.coverage_note:
Ran 10 distinct WebSearch queries (exceeding the requested 6): general viral/bucket-list terms, a site:tiktok.com query, attraction-trend query, architecture boat tour, reddit-tourist query, plus targeted follow-ups on Skydeck Ledge, the Rat Hole, the 'most beautiful city' trend, Shermann Dilla Thomas, Museum of Ice Cream, 360 TILT pricing, Color Factory, WNDR Museum, the Bean, and Riverwalk kayaking.

Real limits: WebSearch returns Google-indexed summaries of TikTok discover/video pages, not the TikTok app or API itself — I could not pull actual view counts, like counts, or verify handles beyond what appeared in search snippets (a few counts did surface, e.g. WNDR's 86K likes/16.3K followers, one Museum of Ice Cream video's 99.9K likes, and Chicago's cited '17.9 billion TikTok views' as a destination — these are third-party-reported figures I did not independently verify against TikTok itself). Ticket prices are as reported by search results/aggregators as of this sweep (Aug 2026) and should be reconfirmed on the venue's own site before booking, since these attractions run frequent promos and seasonal pricing changes.

Notably, the Chicago Rat Hole — probably the single most viral Chicago-specific TikTok phenomenon of 2024 — is EXCLUDED from the places list because it was physically removed by the city in April 2024 and no longer exists as a visitable site; I've flagged it here rather than fabricating a listing for a place tourists can no longer go see. If a "closed but famous" entry would still be useful (e.g., pointing people to its former location on Roscoe St near Damen, now just repaved sidewalk), let me know and I can add it back as a photo/curiosity stop.

I did not find strong, TikTok-specific evidence (beyond generic mentions) for some guidebook staples like Navy Pier's Ferris wheel or Lincoln Park Zoo as distinctly TikTok-amplified rather than just generally popular — they appeared in one aggregated listicle-style result but without dedicated trend evidence, so I left them out rather than force weak entries in.

sweeps.angle: Chicago "hidden gems / locals only" TikTok genre — spots aimed at first-time visitors who'd otherwise only see Millennium Park/Navy Pier/Bean. Covers the Pedway, quirky museums, a disguised speakeasy, conservatories, library atriums, underground food courts, and free skyline views.
sweeps.coverage_note: Ran 12 WebSearch queries total (6+ requested, plus follow-ups to chase specific leads). Strong, directly-sourced evidence (individual video URLs, named creators, or press coverage of the TikTok trend) exists for: Chicago Magic Lounge, Winter Garden/Harold Washington Library, HeungSeng Square underground food court, Garden of the Phoenix, the Chicago Pedway, and Shermann 'Dilla' Thomas's tours. Moderate evidence (aggregated TikTok discover-page tags and secondary write-ups referencing TikTok virality, but no single pinned high-view video) covers Garfield Park Conservatory, International Museum of Surgical Science, and the free-skyline-view spots. Weak evidence (name surfaced once in an aggregated search summary, no direct TikTok video or creator identified) covers Undercover Books, Armadillo's Pillow, 12th Street Beach, and Luella's Southern Kitchen — these should be treated as plausible leads worth a follow-up TikTok-app search, not confirmed viral spots. WebSearch cannot browse TikTok's app directly or pull view/like counts, so "virality" here is inferred from discover-page existence, named creators, and press coverage, not hard engagement numbers. Also flagging: a separate, more sensational "Underground Chicago" tunnel trend went viral in 2025 but was substantially debunked by WBEZ/Sun-Times as conflating real (but off-limits/decaying) freight tunnels with the legitimate, walkable Pedway — I kept the Pedway entry but noted the distinction rather than platform the debunked framing. Not covered in this sweep due to time: an in-app TikTok search (would need the TikTok skill/API rather than WebSearch) for harder view-count verification, and neighborhood-specific gems in Pilsen, Bridgeport, and Albany Park.

sweeps.angle: Chicago food spots (2024-2026) with documented or plausible TikTok virality — spanning the "critic visit" phenomenon (Keith Lee), single-dish giant/cheese-pull format spots, and the classic Chicago trio (deep dish, Italian beef, Chicago dog)
sweeps.coverage_note: TikTok has no public search API and its own web/discover pages surface mostly generic hashtag pages rather than individual high-view videos, so I could not pull hard view-count numbers for most entries directly from TikTok itself. Where I cite a specific view/like count, it came from a secondary source (news article or a search-engine-summarized TikTok result) — I've flagged those. Two entries (Frato's giant mozzarella stick and Limoni Belli's chicken parm sandwich) are included because they fit the requested 'giant/oversized/cheese-pull' format exactly, but I marked them 'weak' evidence because I could not verify an actual originating viral video or creator for either — the virality claim exists in food-roundup coverage but I couldn't source it further upstream. I was not able to find a strong single-dish deep-dish 'giant slice' viral moment (e.g., a specific record-setting slice video) — the deep dish entries here (Pequod's, Lou Malnati's) are backed by recurring comparison-format content rather than one breakout clip. I did not find documented evidence for a viral Chicago dog spot beyond Portillo's (Keith Lee visit) and the general #chicagohotdog hashtag volume — no single Chicago-dog-specific restaurant emerged with strong dedicated virality the way Kong Dog or Ed Debevic's did. I ran 14 distinct searches as requested but did not use claude-in-chrome to browse TikTok directly (no live browser session was opened for this task), which likely limited discovery of view-count-specific evidence beyond what search engines already indexed.

sweeps.angle: Chinese-language (TikTok/抖音/小红书) creator coverage of Chicago, 2024-2026 — contrasted against English-language coverage. The Chinese-language lens skews toward: 打卡 (photo check-in) landmarks with mirror/reflection or oversized-scale visual appeal (The Bean, Starbucks Reserve, 360 Chicago tilt), 人均 (per-person spend) framing for food, heavy emphasis on Chinatown/Asian food as a home-base for Chinese travelers and international students, and practical logistics content (parking, how to get deep-dish takeout, "芝加哥必吃三样" listicle formats). English-language TikTok coverage skews more toward individual creator "must-try" restaurant hauls (Crying Tiger, Chubby Cattle) and novelty spots (Hello Kitty Cafe) that have NOT surfaced in Chinese-language search results at all — suggesting a real language-market gap rather than universal virality.
sweeps.coverage_note: Direct TikTok/抖音 in-app search was not possible — this research was done entirely via WebSearch, which surfaces Chinese travel-blog, Dealmoon, Zhihu, Douban, Ctrip/Qunar, and Baidu-indexed aggregator content that itself references or is downstream of TikTok/Douyin/Xiaohongshu virality, plus a small number of direct TikTok hashtag/discover pages. This is a real limitation: for several places (Garrett Popcorn, deep dish, Starbucks Reserve, Old Joliet Prison) I found strong evidence they ARE circulated as 网红/爆红 (viral check-in) content in the Chinese travel-content ecosystem broadly, but could not pull specific view counts, named creators, or individual video URLs the way a logged-in TikTok/Douyin session could. I flagged evidence_strength accordingly (moderate rather than strong) wherever the link to TikTok/Douyin specifically, versus Chinese social media/travel blogs generally, was inferred rather than directly confirmed. Also not found in this sweep despite searching: any dedicated Xiaohongshu-native content (searches returned mentions of 小红书 virality but not actual 小红书 post URLs, since Xiaohongshu is not well-indexed by general web search). English-language-only TikTok trends (Crying Tiger, Chubby Cattle, Hello Kitty Cafe, Louis Vuitton Cafe) surfaced clearly in English search but did NOT appear anywhere in the Chinese-language searches — reported as a genuine market gap, not an oversight. No results were fabricated; every place listed appeared by name in at least one search result above.

sweeps.angle: Chicago dessert / cafe / bubble tea / brunch spots trending on TikTok, 2024-2026
sweeps.coverage_note: Ran 16 WebSearch queries (double the required 6), covering dessert, cafe/aesthetic, bakery/croissant, brunch, boba, and donut/cookie angles specifically. All evidence comes from WebSearch result summaries of TikTok video/discover pages and a few corroborating local press pieces (WTTW, Axios, Secret Chicago) — I did not browse TikTok directly, so I cannot confirm exact view/like counts on any individual video; evidence_strength reflects how directly and repeatedly TikTok content named each spot as 'viral' vs. just appearing in generic roundups. One spot I deliberately excluded after checking: Saint Honoré Doughnuts is heavily TikTok-viral but is fundamentally a Las Vegas-based brand (people are shown flying in from elsewhere to try it) — its Chicago presence is unconfirmed/unclear, so I left it out rather than misrepresent it as a Chicago spot. I could not verify current operating status, wait times, or recent negative-review pileups (the 'viral-then-mediocre' pattern the brief asked about) beyond what's noted in practical_tip for Ume Tea and Do-Rite Donuts — a deeper Yelp/Reddit cross-check would sharpen those calls further if needed. Brunch category is thinner than the others (only Honeybear Cafe had strong specific-item evidence); Recess and Tortoise Supper Club appeared in results but without a specific viral dish/angle, so I omitted them rather than pad the list with weak entries.

dropped.name: WNDR Museum
dropped.reason: The single most damaging error a travel guide can make: WNDR Museum announced it is permanently closing September 7, 2026 (confirmed via WNDR's own Instagram/Facebook farewell post and ABC7 Chicago coverage, plus its Boston sister location closing the same date). As of today (Aug 19, 2026) it is still technically open for about 3 more weeks, but any guide with a shelf life beyond that is sending people to a closed building. Do not recommend without an explicit, prominent closure date warning — safer to drop entirely.

dropped.name: Chicago Riverwalk / Millennium Park "Beautiful City" skyline shot
dropped.reason: This entry is not a place — it duplicates the Riverwalk and Millennium Park entries already listed separately in this set, wrapped around an unverifiable TikTok ranking claim ('2nd most beautiful city in the world') that the input itself already flags as unsourced. Since the underlying locations are already covered as their own KEEP entries, this duplicate trend-format entry should be dropped rather than double-counted as a distinct attraction.

dropped.name: Gangnam Market (soccer ball ice cream)
dropped.reason: Wrong neighborhood: Gangnam Market is in River West at 1001 W. Chicago Ave, not Chinatown - roughly 3 miles away, a different part of the city entirely. Additionally, the specific 'soccer ball ice cream' claim could not be verified; the closest corroborated product is fruit-shaped ice cream from Aiko Garden, a different shape and framing than the input claimed. Sending readers to Chinatown for this item would be a wasted trip.

dropped.name: Hyde Park
dropped.reason: The input itself flags this as low-confidence: no verified viral walk route or named business surfaced, only generic 'vs downtown' comparison content and a Juneteenth-event mention. This does not meet the bar for a TikTok-driven neighborhood recommendation - it reads as a filler entry padding out the list rather than a substantiated spot.

dropped.name: Amici
dropped.reason: Confirmed closed. Block Club Chicago reported April 20, 2026 that the owner is retiring and closing Amici — the same viral lifeline restaurant that briefly boomed after Keith Lee's July 2024 visit. This is exactly the single most damaging error a guide can make: recommending a place that no longer exists.

dropped.name: Limoni Belli
dropped.reason: This fails the evidence bar on two counts: (1) the original TikTok claim was already flagged as unverifiable by the sourcing agent and remains unverifiable after independent search — no originating creator, video, or view count found anywhere, only aggregator sites repeating the claim as fact; (2) the review base is thin (Yelp shows only 17 reviews at the associated address), which is not enough signal to recommend confidently in a guide that claims viral status. A mobile-only operation with no verifiable virality claim and a thin review base does not clear the bar for inclusion.

dropped.name: Secret hiking skyline overlook (likely Cricket Hill, Montrose Point / Uptown)
dropped.reason: The underlying claim is unverifiable as written — no confirmed location, no address, no way to send a traveler somewhere specific. Fabricating a pin (even a plausible one like Cricket Hill) to fill the gap would misrepresent unverified content as a confirmed recommendation.
